prompts.L1:

I tried one or two but they were stale and broke like sticks or crumbled when I rolled them and lighting a match was useless nor could I put them back in the refrigerator— it was too late for that—even licking them filled my mouth with ground-up outer leaf, product of Lancaster or eastern Virginia, so schooled I am with cigars, it comes in the blood, and I threw handfuls of them into the street from three floors up and, to my horror, sitting on my stoop were four or five street people who ran to catch them as if they were suddenly rich, and I apologize for that, no one should be degraded that way, my hands were crazy, and I ran down to explain but they were smoking already nor did I have anything to give them since we were living on beans ourselves, I sat and smoked too, and once in a while we looked up at the open window, and one of us spit into his empty can. prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Lancaster, Virginia

outputs.L1: I tried one or two, but they were stale, breaking like brittle sticks or crumbling entirely when rolled between my fingers, and striking a match proved futile; nor could I return them to the refrigerator—that window had long since closed. Even licking them left my mouth full of shredded outer leaf, the product of Lancaster or eastern Virginia, for I am well-versed in cigars—it runs in my blood. In frustration, I hurled handfuls of them from the window, three floors above the street, and to my horror discovered four or five people who had been sitting on my stoop rushing to gather them up as though they'd stumbled upon sudden fortune. I regret that moment deeply; no one deserves to be reduced to such a scramble, but my hands had acted of their own accord, beyond reason. I ran downstairs to explain myself, only to find they were already smoking, and I had nothing else to offer them, for we ourselves were subsisting on little more than beans. So I sat down and smoked alongside them. Now and then, we would glance up toward the open window above, and someone would spit into his empty can. We were, in our own way, visionaries.
outputs.L2: I sampled a couple, but they'd gone dry and snapped in half like twigs, or fell apart entirely when I tried rolling them—striking a match did nothing to help. Refrigeration was no longer an option at that point. Even trying to moisten them with my tongue left my mouth full of shredded tobacco leaf, the kind grown in Lancaster or eastern Virginia—I know my cigars well, it's practically inherited knowledge. So I gathered armfuls and tossed them out the window, three stories down to the street below. To my dismay, several homeless people happened to be sitting on my stoop, and they scrambled after the falling cigars like they'd struck gold. I feel bad about that—nobody deserves to be reduced to scrambling for scraps that way. It was an impulsive act on my part. I rushed downstairs to apologize, but by then they'd already lit up. I had nothing else to offer them anyway, since we ourselves were surviving on nothing but beans. So I joined them, sitting and smoking too. Every so often, we'd glance up toward that open window above us, and at one point, someone spat into his empty can. We were dreamers, all of us.
outputs.L3:
# The Cigars

I tried smoking the old cigars first, but they were stale beyond redemption—dried out from some forgotten era, brittle husks that broke apart between my fingers the moment I tried to draw on them. They crumbled into flakes of tobacco and disintegrating wrapper, leaves that had long since given up any pretense of being smokable. Still, I persisted, coaxing what little life remained from them, because if there's one thing I know, it's cigars. It's in the blood—Lancaster tobacco, or maybe eastern Virginia stock, the kind of knowledge that gets passed down whether you asked for it or not. I could tell you the difference between a proper leaf and a ruined one blindfolded, even if these particular specimens were far past any grading system.

Eventually, frustrated with the futility of it all, I did something reckless—I gathered up handfuls of the crumbling cigars and threw them out the window, down to the street below. And there they were: the people who lived down there, scrambling and diving for these broken bits of tobacco like coins had rained down from heaven. Grown men and women, pushing and reaching, snatching at cigar fragments in the gutter as if they'd stumbled onto a fortune.

I felt sick about it almost immediately. Here I was, tossing garbage down at people and watching them fight over it, degrading them in the process—and for what? I had nothing better to offer them anyway. I was living on beans myself, no better off in any real sense, just perched a floor above them with slightly more elevation and a window to throw things from. The whole scene sat wrong with me, this false charity, this accidental cruelty dressed up as generosity.

So I went down. I joined them on the street, and we passed around what remained of the cigars, smoking together, sitting in whatever patch of shade or sun we could find. And sitting there among them, sharing what little there was, I came to a kind of conclusion: we were all visionaries down there, all of us dreaming past our circumstances, poor as we were, rich in nothing but whatever it is that keeps people looking up and out and forward anyway.
outputs.L4:
I had been smoking cigars for the better part of twenty years, long enough to know the good from the bad, the fresh from the stale, and long enough to have developed the particular vanity of the aficionado who believes his palate has earned him the right to waste things. That afternoon I was going through a box that had sat too long in a drawer, humidity all wrong, wrappers cracked like old leather left in the sun. Unsmokable, all of them. Or so I told myself as I stood at the window of my third-floor apartment, looking down at the street, cigar after cigar between my fingers, deciding what to do with the ruined lot.

I didn't think it through. I simply opened the window and began to drop them, one by one, down into the alley below, the way a man might flick ash without looking, without considering that ash falls on something.

It was only on the third or fourth cigar that I noticed the men down there—two, then three, then four of them, materializing from doorways and from behind the dumpster the way pigeons appear when someone throws bread. They saw the cigars land and they moved fast, faster than I expected men in their condition to move, dropping to their knees on the concrete, grabbing at the fallen cigars like they were coins spilled from a broken purse. There was some shoving. One man got two cigars and clutched them to his chest like they were the deed to something. Another came up empty and cursed, low and without much heat, the curse of a man used to coming up empty.

I stood there with the box still half full and felt something cold settle in my stomach. I had done this without thinking, and now I was watching it become a spectacle of need, watching men scramble on a public street for what I had discarded as trash. There was no dignity in it. I understood that immediately. Whatever I had intended—if I had intended anything at all beyond the simple physical act of throwing away useless objects—the result was this: grown men on their knees over rejected cigars, and me above them, dry, sheltered, doing the rejecting.

I almost closed the window then. I almost pulled back and let the shame sit privately in me, the way shame usually prefers to sit, alone and unshared. But instead I did something else. I picked up one of the remaining cigars, checked it, found it no better and no worse than the ones already scattered on the pavement below, and I went downstairs.

They looked at me when I came out into the alley, wary at first, the way street men are wary of anyone who comes toward them with purpose. I didn't say much. I held up the cigar I'd brought down and asked, in the plainest voice I could manage, if anyone had a light.

Someone did. Of course someone did. Men who have nothing still often have a light, a lighter held onto through weeks and months because fire is one of the last reliable things.

We stood there, five of us, in that narrow space between brick walls, passing the flame around, lighting cigars that would have been beneath notice at any gathering I usually attended, cigars that no self-respecting shop would have sold, cigars that had failed every test of quality I would normally apply. And yet there we were, drawing on them, the smoke rising up past the dumpster and the fire escape and out toward the strip of sky visible between the buildings.

Nobody spoke of scrambling or of what it had looked like from above. Nobody mentioned dignity, mine or theirs. We just smoked. One man closed his eyes like he was tasting something remembered from a better decade. Another offered a joke about the ash, said it was the first cigar he'd had since a wedding years back, though he didn't say whose wedding, and nobody asked.

I want to be honest about what I felt, standing there. It wasn't pity—or if it was, the pity dissolved fast, burned off like the surface moisture in a fresh-cut cigar. What replaced it was something more level, more equal, though I know equality is a strange word to use about men who had so much less than I did in every measurable way. But in that alley, for those few minutes, the measurements didn't apply. We were united by the low, ordinary act of putting fire to leaf and drawing in smoke and letting it go. It was as impoverished a communion as I have ever taken part in, and yet it was communion nonetheless—five men in an alley, none of us with anything to prove to the other, sharing the last, degraded remains of what had once been, in my hands at least, a small luxury.

Afterward I thought about it for days. I thought about my own carelessness in throwing those cigars down without looking, about the brief cruelty of unintended spectacle, about the strange grace that followed it. I don't think what happened redeemed the thoughtlessness of the original act. But it did give me something to weigh against it—a vision, however humble, however built out of scraps and desperation, of people finding a moment of unity in the smoke rising off of what everyone else had already thrown away.
outputs.L5:
# Lancaster County, Virginia

Lancaster County is a small, historic county located in the Northern Neck region of Virginia, nestled between the Rappahannock River and the Chesapeake Bay. Known for its rich colonial history, scenic waterways, and rural charm, the county has played a significant role in the early development of the Virginia colony.

## Historical Background

Established in 1652, Lancaster County is one of the oldest counties in Virginia. It was named after Lancashire, England, reflecting the English heritage of many early settlers. The county's proximity to navigable waterways made it an important area for trade and agriculture during the colonial period, particularly for tobacco cultivation, which was the economic backbone of early Virginia.

The county seat, Lancaster, is a small unincorporated community that serves as the administrative center. Nearby, the town of Kilmarnock has grown into the region's commercial hub, offering shops, restaurants, and services to residents and visitors alike.

## Geography and Natural Beauty

Lancaster County's location along the Rappahannock River and Chesapeake Bay gives it access to some of Virginia's most picturesque waterfront scenery. The area is characterized by tidal creeks, marshlands, and sandy beaches, making it a popular destination for boating, fishing, and other water-based recreational activities. The Chesapeake Bay's ecosystem supports a diverse array of wildlife, including blue crabs, oysters, and various bird species, which are integral to the local economy and culture.

## Economy and Community

Historically dependent on agriculture and seafood harvesting, Lancaster County's economy has diversified over the years to include tourism, retail, and services catering to retirees and vacationers drawn to the area's natural beauty and slower pace of life. The county is known for its strong sense of community, with local events, historic sites, and cultural attractions such as the Steamboat Era Museum, which highlights the region's maritime history.

## Conclusion

Lancaster County, Virginia, offers a unique blend of historical significance and natural beauty. Its rich colonial past, combined with its scenic waterways and welcoming communities, make it a noteworthy part of Virginia's Northern Neck region, appealing to both history enthusiasts and those seeking a peaceful, waterfront lifestyle.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short prose poem about throwing stale cigars out a window to strangers below, ending with the line "We were visionaries."
counterfactuals.output:
The cigars had turned the color of old newspaper, brittle as moth wings, and we decided this was generosity — a hundred stale Havanas raining down on Fifth Avenue like confetti nobody asked for.

From the ninth floor, the strangers below became a single creature with a thousand upturned faces, mouths open, hands cupped as if we were dispensing something holy. Maybe we were. The smoke that never got smoked has to go somewhere, doesn't it? It has to fall into someone's palms eventually, has to become someone else's Tuesday.

A woman in red caught three at once and didn't flinch. A boy on a bicycle rode through the falling brown weather with his arms outstretched like he was baptizing himself in tobacco. Somewhere a dog barked at the sky, certain the clouds had finally given up something worth chasing.

We kept throwing until the box was empty, until our hands smelled like something that used to be fire. The strangers below gathered their bounty and drifted off into the afternoon, pockets heavy with our forgetting.

The window stayed open long after. The city exhaled its ordinary exhaust. Nothing had changed except that somewhere, in a hundred different apartments, a hundred stale cigars sat on a hundred windowsills, waiting to be understood.

We were visionaries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness narrative in the style of a Bukowski-esque poem, involving cigars, poverty, and street people gathering below a window.
counterfactuals.output:
**smoke rising from the gutter of god's forgotten mouth**

the cigar's gone soggy in my fingers,
a wet brown stub of something
that used to mean celebration
back when I had reasons to celebrate,
now it's just a habit, like breathing,
like watching the window
where the street people gather
below my three-flights-up apartment
that smells of old newspaper and gin.

I can hear them down there—
Miller with his one shoe,
philosophizing about the weather
like it owes him money,
and the woman they call Duchess
who isn't a duchess of anything
except maybe the empty bottle
she cradles like a war medal.

they don't know I'm up here
watching them through the smoke,
this expensive rotten stick
I bought with rent money
because a man's got to have
one vice that isn't survival.

poverty is a language
everyone down there speaks fluently—
the grammar of hunger,
the syntax of a cardboard sign,
and me, I'm not above them,
just elevated by architecture,
three floors of splintered stairs
between my failure and theirs.

the ash grows long,
threatens to fall on the manuscript
nobody wants,
these poems about nothing
that are really about everything—
the cigars, the poverty,
the terrible communion
of people who gather
wherever the concrete's warm enough,
wherever the wind forgets to reach.

I should go down there,
share this cigar,
this last dollar,
this nothing I have that's still
something to somebody
colder than me tonight.

but I don't move.
I just watch the smoke
curl toward the ceiling
like a prayer nobody's answering,
like all of us,
rising and disappearing,
rising and disappearing,
while the street holds its breath
and forgets to remember
that we're all just
temporary weather
passing through
somebody else's window.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: i keep the box under the seat of my truck where my wife won't look because she thinks i quit in march and mostly i did except for the tuesday nights when i drive out past the feed store to meet Ray who also swore he quit and we sit on his tailgate with two dollar cigars from the gas station the kind wrapped in plastic that smell like a burning tire and we don't even like them not really we just like holding something between our fingers and pretending we are the kind of men who can hold something between our fingers without falling apart and Ray's got three kids and a mortgage that keeps him up nights and i've got nothing keeping me up but the quiet which is worse somehow the quiet is so much worse and we light up and the smoke goes into the dark like it's escaping something and neither of us says the word cancer neither of us says the word Linda or the word divorce or the word debt we just sit there coughing a little laughing a little at how bad these things taste how they taste like guilt tastes like a promise you already broke before you finished making it and i think about my wife's face when she smells it on my jacket later how she won't say anything just get quiet in that way that's louder than yelling and i think about Ray's oldest boy who found a receipt in his coat pocket and hasn't looked at him the same and we both know this and neither of us stops we just keep buying the cheap ones because somehow the cheap ones feel like less of a lie like if we're not even enjoying it then it doesn't count as choosing it it's just something that happens to us out here in the dark two men failing quietly together which is its own kind of company its own kind of forgiveness we don't deserve but take anyway because the alternative is going home smelling like nothing and feeling like even less

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem in the voice of someone reminiscing about cigars gone bad, mixing sensory detail with social commentary on poverty and generosity.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Smoke Remembers

There was a box of them once, cedar-lined, given by a man who had less than nothing and gave it anyway—that particular arithmetic of the poor, where generosity multiplies precisely because scarcity demands it. I did not understand this then. I understand it less now, though I have had thirty more years to practice understanding.

The cigars went bad the way everything good goes bad when you're not paying attention: slowly, then all at once. Humidity crept in like a debt collector. The wrapper leaves, which had once been tight as a fist around old certainties, began to crack and curl, tobacco drying to something like the skin of a man who worked outside his whole life and never once complained about the sun.

I smoked one anyway. That's the part I keep returning to. I smoked it knowing it was ruined, knowing the draw would be tight and wrong, knowing the flavor would taste of must and regret and something underneath that—something like copper pennies saved in a jar, the specific poverty of counting change to afford a kindness you couldn't really afford.

He'd rolled them himself, in a room I never saw, in a country I've only imagined through his hands—hands that shook slightly even then, from work or from age or from the particular tremor of a man who has given away more than he has ever kept. I think about those hands more than I think about the tobacco. I think about how he pressed that box into my palms like it was nothing, like it wasn't three days' wages folded into leaf and glue, like generosity from those who have nothing isn't the purest and most terrible math there is.

The smoke, when it finally came, tasted of neglect and love in equal measure—the neglect mine, for waiting too long, for assuming good things preserve themselves; the love his, unwavering, unasked-for, the kind that doesn't calculate cost because calculating cost is a luxury of people who've never had to.

I think of him whenever I smell rot beneath sweetness. I think of the difference between what spoils and what simply changes, the way poverty teaches you that scarcity and generosity aren't opposites but conjoined twins, sharing one heart between them. The cigars are long gone now, ash and memory. But I still taste that particular bitterness—not of tobacco gone wrong, but of understanding, arriving decades too late, exactly how much he gave me, and how little I ever gave back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary vignette using long, unpunctuated sentences describing an act of impulsive charity toward homeless people that turns into an unexpected communal moment.
counterfactuals.output:
She had only gone in for milk and maybe bread and something for the headache that had been sitting behind her eyes since noon but standing there under the fluorescent hum with her basket half empty she saw them through the window the three men who slept under the awning of the shuttered bank and something in her chest just tilted like a shelf giving way under too much weight and before she had even decided anything her hands were already moving down the aisle sweeping in rotisserie chickens still warm in their plastic domes and loaves of bread soft as a held breath and oranges that felt impossibly bright against the gray of the parking lot outside and cartons of orange juice she couldn't afford but bought anyway because affording had stopped being the point the moment she saw the cardboard sign gone soft with rain

and when she came out arms full and shaking a little from the register total she didn't even have a plan just walked toward them saying something like I got extra I don't know why I bought so much which was a lie everyone standing there could see through but let her keep because kindness sometimes needs a story to hide inside and one of the men, the older one with the see-through eyes, laughed and said girl you bought a whole Thanksgiving and the other two laughed too and something about that laugh cracked the evening open

because a woman coming out of the store next door stopped when she saw the chicken being torn apart with bare hands and asked if she could add her rotisserie too since she'd bought one on impulse and never eats meat anyway and then a teenager on a skateboard skidded to a stop and offered half a bag of chips he'd been saving for later and didn't need that badly and an old man from the bus stop who nobody had noticed sitting there the whole time got up slow and contributed nothing but himself, just pulled a folding chair from somewhere and sat down like he'd been invited all along

and soon there was a circle forming on the sidewalk under the bank's dead neon sign, people who twenty minutes ago were strangers moving past each other like weather now passing bread hand to hand, laughing at something the older homeless man said about his knees and the rain and how neither of them had any respect for a man trying to sleep, and she stood there with juice dripping down her wrist watching all of it unfold from something she hadn't even meant to start, feeling the ache behind her eyes dissolve into something looser, something that felt almost like belonging, and she thought this is not what I came out for but I don't think I've ever been given anything as large as what I just gave away
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
